title: Independence and finiteness of character eigenspaces
statement: Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure], and let $G$ be an affine group scheme [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type over $k$ [def-weil-finite-type-morphism]. Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional $k$-vector space and $r:G\to\operatorname{GL}(V)$ a homomorphism of group schemes, where $\operatorname{GL}(V)$ is the general linear group [def-sc-general-linear-group] after choosing a basis when $\dim_kV>0$; for $V=0$, $\operatorname{GL}(V)$ denotes the trivial group scheme, with $\operatorname{GL}(V)(A)=\operatorname{Aut}_A(0)=\{1\}$. Tensor products are those of [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product], and finite-dimensionality means [def-weil-finite-dimensional-subspace]. A subspace $W\subseteq V$ is $G$-stable if $r_A(g)(A\otimes_kW)\subseteq A\otimes_kW$ for every commutative $k$-algebra $A$ and $g\in G(A)$. A character is a group-scheme homomorphism $\chi:G\to\mathbf G_m$, with $\mathbf G_m=\operatorname{GL}_1$. For each character $\chi$, define $V_\chi=\{v\in V: r_A(g)(1\otimes v)=\chi_A(g)(1\otimes v)\text{ for every commutative }k\text{-algebra }A\text{ and }g\in G(A)\}$. The family of subspaces $(V_\chi)_\chi$ is independent: for any pairwise distinct characters $\chi_1,\ldots,\chi_t$ and vectors $v_i\in V_{\chi_i}$, the equality $\sum_i v_i=0$ implies $v_i=0$ for every $i$. Consequently only finitely many $V_\chi$ are nonzero, and the sum of all the character eigenspaces is their internal direct sum. Neither commutativity, smoothness nor connectedness of $G$ is assumed.

source.place: Theorem 4.25 and Corollary 4.24, printed pp.93–94; finite-dimensionality gives finiteness of the nonzero independent summands.

proof.text: Put $C=k[G]$, so $G=\operatorname{Spec}C$. The maps $\Delta,\varepsilon$ induced by multiplication and identity make $C$ a coalgebra by [lem-sfb-affine-group-coordinate-hopf]. For a character $\chi$, let $a_\chi=\chi^*(t)\in C^\times$, where $k[\mathbf G_m]=k[t,t^{-1}]$. The multiplication and identity formulas for $\operatorname{GL}_1$ give $\Delta(a_\chi)=a_\chi\otimes a_\chi$ and $\varepsilon(a_\chi)=1$, since $\chi$ respects multiplication and identity. Distinct characters give distinct $a_\chi$: a $k$-algebra map from $k[t,t^{-1}]$ is determined by its value on $t$, and affine-spectrum duality says that equal coordinate maps give equal scheme morphisms.

source.place: Chapter 4(g), printed pp.92–93: characters and group-like elements, before Proposition 4.23.

proof.text: Let $u\in G(C)$ be the point corresponding to $\mathrm{id}_C$. Define $\rho:V\to C\otimes_kV$ by $\rho(v)=r_C(u)(1\otimes v)$. This is $k$-linear because $v\mapsto1\otimes v$ is $k$-linear and the fixed operator $r_C(u)$ is $C$-linear. The point $\chi_C(u)$ is $a_\chi$, by evaluation of $\chi^*$ at $\mathrm{id}_C$. Taking $A=C$ and $g=u$ in the defining all-algebras condition for $V_\chi$ gives $\rho(v)=a_\chi\otimes v$ for every $v\in V_\chi$. For $V=0$ the same map is the zero map. Thus no construction of a coaction, nor any reducedness or density of $G(k)$, is needed.

source.place: Proposition 4.22 and equation (28), printed p.92; the coaction on vectors is evaluated at the universal point.

proof.text: Fix pairwise distinct $\chi_1,\ldots,\chi_t$ and $v_i\in V_{\chi_i}$ with $\sum_i v_i=0$. Linearity and step 2 give $\sum_i a_{\chi_i}\otimes v_i=0$. For any $k$-linear form $f:V\to k$, the tensor universal property gives the linear map $C\otimes_kV\to C$, $c\otimes v\mapsto f(v)c$. Applying it yields $\sum_i f(v_i)a_{\chi_i}=0$. The elements $a_{\chi_i}$ are pairwise distinct group-like elements by step 1; [lem-sfb-coalgebra-group-like-independent] therefore gives $f(v_i)=0$ for every $i$ and every $f$.

source.place: Theorem 4.25 proof, printed pp.93–94; Proposition 4.23 supplies the independence used there.

proof.text: If some $v_i\ne0$, apply [lem-sfb-linear-map-extension-prescribed-value] with $P=0\subset V$, the zero map $P\to k$, $v=v_i$ and prescribed value $1\in k$. It gives a linear form $f:V\to k$ with $f(v_i)=1$, contradicting step 3. Thus all $v_i=0$, proving the asserted independence, also for the empty family.

source.place: Theorem 4.25, printed p.94: the last contradiction, with separation by linear forms made explicit.

proof.text: Write $d=\dim_kV$. For any finite set $S$ of characters with $V_\chi\ne0$, choose $0\ne w_\chi\in V_\chi$ for $\chi\in S$. These vectors are linearly independent: a scalar relation $\sum_{\chi\in S}c_\chi w_\chi=0$ has each $c_\chi w_\chi=0$ by step 4, hence each $c_\chi=0$ over the field $k$. By [lem-weil-independent-family-card-le-dimension], $|S|\le d$. The set of such characters must be finite: if it were infinite one could successively choose $d+1$ distinct members, giving a finite set violating this bound. This includes $d=0$, when there are no nonzero eigenspaces.

source.place: Theorem 4.25, pp.93–94, followed by its finite-dimensional consequence; dimension bound as in the cited linear-algebra leaf.

proof.text: Each $V_\chi$ is a subspace, since every equation $r_A(g)(1\otimes v)=\chi_A(g)(1\otimes v)$ is $k$-linear in $v$. Let $S$ be the finite set of nonzero eigenspaces from step 5. The sum map $\bigoplus_{\chi\in S}V_\chi\to V$, $(v_\chi)\mapsto\sum_\chi v_\chi$, has image the sum of all character eigenspaces and has zero kernel by step 4. Its injectivity and this image description are exactly that the sum is an internal direct sum. The empty sum is the zero subspace.

source.place: Theorem 4.25, printed pp.93–94: meaning of directness of the sum.
